debates.title: Tougher border enforcement stops people from migrating
debates.context: David Lindstrom argues Agree; Adam Fischer argues Disagree.

documents.speaker: David Lindstrom
documents.content: Okay, so the question as to whether nation states can impact or control migration to a significant extent has been one of the principle research questions of the global sociology of migration since about the 1970s. And through the end of the Cold War and in the 1990s, the general consensus was that the rural states do not control migration. In fact, it's the economies that control the migration and the policies can make some small impacts here and there, but they really don't have as large an impact as the history of economic connection between different countries, migration networks, conditions in sending and receiving states, etc, etc. I think that the advent of the Trump administration has really changed that. We saw a sharp decrease in migration in response to the harsh border policies starting in 2016 and then continuing through COVID, then a sharp uptick when the Biden administration came in and then a sharp down tick again when the second Trump administration came in. So I think the last 12 years have really caused us to reconsider this question.

documents.speaker: Adam Fischer
documents.content: Yeah, interesting. I think people think that tougher border means that people are gonna stop migrating. I just think that they might stop migrating from one border or from in a very specific way. But they'll probably find new ways, new borders to come. At least I think in France, I'd be curious on the actual statistics. But I think in Europe in general, trying to reinforce borders hasn't really necessarily been successful. Maybe also because it's very difficult thing to actually enact. You end up spending a lot of resources without actually having major stops to the migration. I think as you said, migration is very much, there's an economic draw and people are basically always gonna find a way to migrate. So it kind of leaves the reason for leaving intact.

documents.speaker: David Lindstrom
documents.content: >> I think what you've highlighted is the difficulty of scope conditions. And the scope conditions between the Western US context in Europe are very, very different. You have a much greater political centralization in the United States than you do in Europe. The venues or pathways of migration are probably more limited. We have certain choke points on the Mexican border. Those choke points are interrupted by natural barriers like the desert. And so I do think the scope conditions impact whether or not tough border enforcement impacts migration. And I think that's always going to be the case. And probably the research question has to be addressed by first setting out the scope conditions.

documents.speaker: Adam Fischer
documents.content: counter arguments as well is it can encourage people to stay permanently. So I think there's been some research on Mexico and US migration that found that tougher enforcement, this scourge migrants to kind of return home. And so if crossing becomes expensive and dangerous, people are discouraged to do it. And therefore, enforcement actually helps turn migration into kind of permanent settlement. I think it was like Princeton research. And I feel like that's, yeah, I'd be curious to know what you think about that.

documents.speaker: David Lindstrom
documents.content: >> Yeah, so you're talking about Douglas Massey's work, which found that the increased enforcement of the border migration caused circular migration to become one way migration. And I think that the Trump administration actions have shown is that it cannot only stop people from migrating circularly or from migrating linearly, but it can actually stop the migration at all and as you said, turn it into more permanent settlement. I think that's an accurate characterization.

documents.speaker: Adam Fischer
documents.content: Okay, so I think whilst people think that tougher border enforcement kind of will stop people from migrating, I think the truth is that actually it costs a lot of money, the economic reality is still the same. But it actually probably just creates a negative climate in the country, at least that's how I'm perceiving what's happening in the US. I don't, kicking out of enforcing border has not been a good thing. Enforcing border hasn't actually really changed much from where I stand, it's more.

documents.content: Okay, so I disagreed with this proposition because I think it's too categorical. There's really two propositions here, right? People are smarter than ever, and people are taking judgments into their own hands more than ever. With respect to intelligence, I think AI is changing things quite a bit. I think it capacitates people who have their own knowledge fund that was created prior to AI and it capacitates them to work more effectively by testing frameworks, searching literatures more effectively, doing those sorts of things. I think it has the capacity to prevent, especially young people who haven't invented their own funded knowledge, to develop that before working with AI and actually make them less intelligent. And this leads us to the second proposition. And it seems to me that people that are highly capacitated with their own funded knowledge and using AI can take more on to themselves in terms of their judgment and do so effectively.
